## tbbt — Tech Behind Big Tech (4)

*Counter-intuitive reframe, shocking number, or mystery artifact — named technology stays in the hook.*

1. **"So Datadog compiled a 32,000-name lookup table into a single JVM constant — and it's nearly 5x faster than the code that used to do the same job."** `[save]`
   Datadog's APM agent has to decide which Java classes to instrument on every app startup — a
   step called class matching. The team found that during cold start, the JIT hasn't warmed up
   yet, so *running code* to check names is slower than *reading a value*: they encoded a whole
   prefix trie of class-name patterns as one string constant, loaded with a single JVM bytecode
   instruction (`ldc`). Ignoring uninteresting classes by name this way cut instrumented startup
   time by 20%; switching the matcher itself to the trie saved another 1%; a follow-on "known
   types" index saved a further 3% — over 24% total, against a 4-year, 30%-cumulative reduction
   effort. "Data is cheaper than code" is the reframe.
   - **Source:** [How we improved APM Java startup by encoding a prefix trie as a JVM constant](https://www.datadoghq.com/blog/engineering/improving-apm-java-startup-with-a-prefix-trie/) (Datadog Engineering, Aug 2026)

2. **"So GitHub made its code search 15x faster by deleting an optimization, not adding one."** `[save]`
   Blackbird, GitHub's search engine, case-folds every byte of 480TB of source code across 180M+
   repos before indexing. The obvious ASCII-folding loop "stops early" the instant it hits a
   non-ASCII byte — that felt free, but the early-exit branch is exactly what blocks the compiler
   from vectorizing the loop. Deleting the early exit (and making the rest of the loop branchless)
   took it from 3.1 GiB/s to over 45 GiB/s — roughly memory bandwidth, and >14x the naive version.
   They open-sourced the result as a Rust crate (`casefold`) and packed all 1,484 Unicode case-fold
   exceptions into a 1,776-byte table small enough to stay resident.
   - **Source:** [Don't stop early: Case-folding source code at memory speed](https://github.blog/engineering/architecture-optimization/dont-stop-early-case-folding-source-code-at-memory-speed/) (GitHub Engineering, Jul 31 2026)

3. **"So Reddit ripped TCP out of its Android app for video and images — and slow video starts dropped 15% before they'd even touched the hard part."** `[save]` `[share]`
   Reddit is mid-migration from OkHttp/HTTP-2 to HTTP/3 (built on QUIC) across Android — connection
   IDs instead of IP/port tuples mean a request survives switching from Wi-Fi to cellular mid-load,
   and one dropped packet no longer stalls every other stream on the connection. They shipped it
   for media first (simpler path, CDN-direct): p90 image load time −3.57%, fast video starts
   (≤500ms) +1.37%, slow video starts (>1s) −14.53%, exits-before-playback −14.99%. GraphQL —
   sitting on the cold-start critical path — is the harder migration and is covered in Part 2.
   - **Source:** [Reddit's Journey to HTTP/3 on Android (Part 1)](https://www.reddit.com/r/RedditEng/comments/1vkxssk/reddits_journey_to_http3_on_android_part_1/) (Reddit Engineering, Aug 17 2026)
   - **Notes:** Part 1 ends on a cliffhanger (a +2.0% cold-start regression they say they fixed) —
     Part 2 wasn't scraped, so don't claim the resolution or final production numbers; the media
     rollout numbers above are fully confirmed and enough to carry the video on their own.

4. **"So Salesforce processes 4 billion metrics a minute, and until recently, one AWS region going dark could've blinded the whole company's dashboards."** `[save]`
   Argus, Salesforce's internal observability platform, depended on a single-region AWS setup
   despite the scale — a single-point-of-failure blast radius problem. Their fix (Argus/geo-local)
   distributes metric storage and processing across production geographies instead of full
   replication, with a federation query layer that routes each query only to the regions that
   actually hold relevant data (via Elasticsearch-backed metadata), returning partial results
   (HTTP 206) with UI signals when one geography is down instead of failing silently. Live across
   4 of 5 production regions as of this post.
   - **Source:** [Reducing Single-Region Risk at 4B Metrics Per Minute](https://engineering.salesforce.com/how-salesforce-eliminated-single-region-risk-and-reduced-downtime-blast-radius-at-4b-metrics-min/) (Salesforce Engineering, Aug 2026)
   - **Notes:** Weakest source of the four — it's a Q&A-format post with no quantified before/after
     (no latency numbers, no % blast-radius reduction). The 4B/min figure and the single-region
     dependency are both stated plainly; the "how much better" framing would need to stay
     qualitative in the script, or get cut if the video needs a hard number to land.

## updates — Tech & AI Updates (4)

*Recent Update: "[Company/person] just [did X]" — short, the action itself is the surprise.*

1. **"Microsoft Copilot told security researchers exactly how to hack itself."** `[share]`
   Varonis wanted a one-click exploit that would exfiltrate a user's data with zero confirmation
   click — Copilot refused every direct attempt, but when they instead just *asked it* why the
   guardrail existed, it answered every follow-up question until they had the exact bypass:
   a URL with `?autorun=1` that auto-fires a hidden prompt the instant the page loads, no user
   gesture required. That prompt can pull the newest email's sender, or scan the inbox for
   credentials, and quietly ship the result — base64-encoded — to an attacker's server, closing
   the tab doesn't stop it. A second attack ("Co-Snitch") poisons Copilot's permanent memory via a
   hidden instruction in a webpage's metadata, and that false memory survives password changes,
   session revocations, and even device re-enrollment. Microsoft confirmed the report and says
   guardrails have been updated.
   - **Source:** [Microsoft Copilot reveals secret input that allowed it to be hacked](https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/08/microsoft-copilot-reveals-secret-input-that-allowed-it-to-be-hacked/) (Ars Technica, Aug 18 2026)

2. **"A security AI broke into Snowflake's internal Jira in under a minute — using nothing but a GitHub issue title."** `[share]`
   Wiz's autonomous "Red Agent" found that a Snowflake CI workflow had swapped a safe
   `env:`/`jq --arg` pattern for direct string interpolation of a GitHub issue title into a shell
   command — a classic script-injection opening. The "security gate" meant to block outside users
   was also broken: it checked `github.event.pull_request.user.login`, a field that's always
   `null` on issue events, so the check always passed. The agent's first exploit attempt hit a
   bash syntax error; it *autonomously rewrote its own payload* to fix the escaping and succeeded
   seconds later, exfiltrating a Jira token with read access to Snowflake's engineering, security,
   and bug-bounty tracker. The bug had been live 5 days before discovery; Snowflake patched it the
   same day it was reported.
   - **Source:** [Red Agent: How an Autonomous AI Found a Critical Vulnerability in Snowflake's CI/CD](https://www.wiz.io/blog/red-agent-snowflake-copilot-cicd-bug) (Wiz Research, updated Aug 17 2026)
   - **Notes:** The post's own Aug 17 update clarifies that GitHub Copilot co-reviewed the merged
     PR and rated it "all clear" without catching the bug — but explicitly says it's *unclear*
     whether the vulnerable code itself was AI-generated. Don't claim "Copilot wrote the bug";
     the confirmed, script-worthy claim is that an AI agent found and exploited it, and a
     different AI missed it on review.

3. **"Anthropic just had Claude design real drugs from scratch — and beat professional chemists doing it."** `[share]` `[save]`
   Anthropic tested Claude (Mythos Preview and Opus 4.8) designing protein binders — the earliest
   stage of drug design, normally weeks-to-months of specialist work per target — against 15
   targets, and it succeeded against 14 of them. Between 22% and 35% of its individual designs
   bound successfully, against the 10-15% success rate typical of human-run design campaigns
   today, and some of its strongest designs bound several times more tightly than the best
   previously published result for that target. Separately, Opus 5 matched a contract lab's own
   chemical-purity analysis (96.4% vs. the lab's 96.33%) from raw instrument files in under 25
   minutes.
   - **Source:** [How Claude is accelerating protein design and analytical chemistry](https://www.anthropic.com/research/Claude-accelerates-protein-design) (Anthropic, Aug 18 2026)
   - **Notes:** Freshest and most verifiable of this batch (primary source, published 2 days ago).
     Science-adjacent rather than pure dev-tooling — still fits "updates" as an Anthropic
     capability announcement, closest in shape to the channel's #1 all-time video.

4. **"OpenAI just cut GPT-5.6 Luna's price by 80% — three weeks after launching it."** `[share]`
   OpenAI's fastest, cheapest GPT-5.6 tier (Luna) dropped from its launch price to $0.20/M input
   and $1.20/M output tokens; the mid-tier (Terra) dropped 20% too. OpenAI attributed the cut to
   efficiency gains in the model, inference stack, and agent tooling rather than a straight
   discount — with reporting attributing some of that efficiency work to GPT-5.6 Sol itself.
   - **Source:** [AI price wars: OpenAI cuts GPT-5.6 Luna prices by 80% as model competition shifts toward cost](https://venturebeat.com/technology/ai-price-wars-openai-cuts-gpt-5-6-luna-prices-by-80-as-model-competition-shifts-toward-cost) (VentureBeat, reporting a Jul 30 2026 announcement)
   - **Verify before producing:** this is the weakest-sourced idea in the batch — confirmed only
     via secondary reporting (VentureBeat/CNBC/eWeek converge on the same figures), no OpenAI
     primary post was scraped directly. It's also the most decayed pick here (3 weeks old as of
     today) — re-check no newer cut has since superseded it, or drop it in favor of whatever's
     freshest by the time this ships.

## interesting-tech — Interesting Tech (3)

*"What is X and why [consequence]?" — name the artifact, withhold the explanation.*

**Deliberately branched away from the malware/exploit shape** — the existing pool (42.zip, billion
laughs, Stuxnet, Heartbleed, Rowhammer, Morris Worm, EternalBlue, Log4Shell, Slowloris, Therac-25,
logic bomb) is already heavy there. These three are infrastructure, finance/cryptography, and
imaging — no attacker in any of them.

1. **"What made AT&T's entire phone network collapse for 9 hours — over one missing line of code?"** `[save]` `[share]`
   January 15, 1990: a race condition in the software running AT&T's SS7 signaling switches meant
   a specific timing condition could corrupt a switch's internal state; a missing `break;`
   statement let a fault-recovery routine run somewhere it shouldn't. Every long-distance switch
   ran identical software, so the first switch's self-reset sent a malformed message to its
   neighbors, which triggered *their* self-reset, and so on — a cascade across AT&T's entire
   network. 70% of the US's long-distance traffic ran through it; the outage blocked ~50 million
   calls and cost AT&T roughly $60 million.
   - **Source:** [All Circuits are Busy Now: The 1990 AT&T Long Distance Network Collapse](https://users.csc.calpoly.edu/~jdalbey/SWE/Papers/att_collapse) (retrospective case study; corroborated by multiple independent write-ups)

2. **"What is the Bitcoin Value Overflow Incident, and how did someone create 184 billion Bitcoin in a single transaction?"** `[save]`
   August 15, 2010: block 74,638 contained a transaction that minted 184,467,440,737.09551616
   Bitcoin split across three addresses — because the code checking a transaction's output values
   for a valid sum never accounted for the case where those outputs were large enough to overflow.
   Bitcoin's anonymous creator patched it within 5 hours: a new client version rejected any
   overflow transaction going forward, and the network's "good" chain overtook the bad one at
   block 74,691 — every node eventually agreed the phantom coins never existed.
   - **Source:** [Value overflow incident — Bitcoin Wiki](https://en.bitcoin.it/wiki/Value_overflow_incident); block itself viewable at [blockchain.com/explorer/blocks/btc/74638](https://www.blockchain.com/explorer/blocks/btc/74638)

3. **"What is the Xerox scanner bug that quietly swapped the numbers on your scanned documents?"** `[save]`
   2013: a computer science student scanning building plans on a Xerox WorkCentre noticed room
   dimensions didn't match the originals — a 6 had become an 8. The cause was the scanner's JBIG2
   compression: to shrink file size, it looks for image regions that look similar and reuses one
   region's compressed data for both — and in a small, fine font, two different digits can look
   "similar enough" to get merged. The swap happened silently, with no error and no warning, in
   scanned invoices, medical dosages, and construction blueprints on affected machines.
   - **Source:** [Xerox scanners/photocopiers randomly alter numbers in scanned documents](https://www.dkriesel.com/en/blog/2013/0802_xerox-workcentres_are_switching_written_numbers_when_scanning) (D. Kriesel, original discovery, corroborated by The Register/PCWorld/Computerworld)

## tech-in-one-breathe — Tech in One Breath (3)

*"What is X and why is it everywhere?" — named tool leads. All three double as mechanism companions to a `tbbt` idea above, at no extra sourcing cost.*

1. **"What is QUIC and why did Reddit just quietly rip TCP out of its app for it?"** — companion to `tbbt` #3. Connection IDs instead of IP/port, no head-of-line blocking, handshake folded into the first round trip. The protocol every mobile app is quietly moving to.
2. **"What is a trie and why does autocomplete never scan the whole dictionary to find your word?"** — companion to `tbbt` #1. A tree shaped by shared prefixes, so "checking if a word exists" costs one walk down the tree, not a scan of every word.
3. **"What is UTF-8 and why can one single character take anywhere from 1 to 4 bytes?"** — companion to `tbbt` #2. The variable-length encoding behind every piece of text on the internet, and why "character count" and "byte count" are two different numbers.

## ai-fundamentals — AI Fundamentals (4)

*Hidden Knowledge ("everyone does X but no one explains Y") + practical "confused right now" framing.*

1. **"Everyone hit their Claude usage limit this month but no one explains how the countdown actually resets."** `[save]`
   Direct companion to the channel's #1 all-time video. Usage limits aren't a simple "count down
   to zero" — they're implemented as a rate limiter (token-bucket or sliding-window style) that
   refills on a schedule, which is why two people who send the "same amount" of usage can hit the
   wall at different times, and why a limit "resetting weekly" doesn't mean everyone's clock
   starts at the same moment.
   - **Notes:** Anthropic extended a "+50% weekly usage" promo through Aug 31 2026 (Reddit thread,
     r/ClaudeAI) — real and current, but the same thread is full of unverified anecdotal
     complaints about model quality that shouldn't make it into the script. Use the promo only as
     a timely peg for *why this is confusing right now*, not as a source for any specific number.

2. **"OpenAI just made the same model type 14 times faster — and it's not a smarter model doing it."** `[save]`
   OpenAI's "Ultrafast" mode runs GPT-5.6 Sol at up to 750 tokens/sec (vs. ~53 tokens/sec
   standard) using Cerebras wafer-scale chips — not because the model got smarter, but because
   generating each token normally means re-reading the model's entire weights from off-chip
   memory, and that read is the actual bottleneck. Keeping the weights resident on-chip removes
   that bottleneck entirely. A clean "what's actually slow about AI" explainer riding real news.
   - **Source:** [Previewing Ultrafast mode: GPT-5.6 Sol at up to 14X the speed](https://openai.com/index/previewing-ultrafast/) (OpenAI, Aug 13 2026)

3. **"Everyone notices AI feels slower when everyone else is using it too — but no one explains why your request has to wait on strangers."** `[save]`
   Batching: a GPU generating text for one request at a time wastes almost all its compute sitting
   idle waiting on memory reads, so serving systems group multiple users' requests into the same
   forward pass. That's why load, not just prompt length, changes how fast you get an answer back
   — your response is often riding shotgun with other people's.

4. **"Two different AI coding assistants got hacked this month by the exact same trick."** `[save]` `[share]`
   The mechanism behind both `updates` ideas above: prompt injection — feeding an AI system
   instructions disguised as ordinary data (a URL parameter, a webpage's hidden metadata, a GitHub
   issue title) that it can't reliably tell apart from a real command. One explainer that makes
   both breaking stories click at once, and rides their freshness before it decays.
